name: Pigmented villonodular synovitis (tenosynovial giant cell tumour)
aliases: giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath

clinicalPearls: A benign but locally aggressive proliferative disorder of the synovium, now classified within the tenosynovial giant cell tumour family
Occurs in localised (nodular) and diffuse forms, with the diffuse type being more aggressive and prone to recurrence
Usually monoarticular, most often affecting the knee, and typically presents in young to middle-aged adults with pain, swelling and recurrent effusions
Aspiration classically yields serosanguineous or brown (haemosiderin-stained) joint fluid, reflecting recurrent haemarthrosis
MRI is the investigation of choice and shows haemosiderin-laden proliferative synovium with characteristic low signal and 'blooming' artefact on gradient-echo sequences
Driven in most cases by overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1), providing the rationale for CSF1R-directed therapy in advanced or unresectable disease
Primary treatment is surgical synovectomy, with radiotherapy or CSF1R inhibition considered for diffuse, recurrent or inoperable disease
reference.pathophysiology: Pigmented villonodular synovitis is a neoplastic proliferation of the synovial lining producing villous and nodular thickening with abundant haemosiderin-laden macrophages, multinucleated giant cells and foam cells. The majority of cases are driven by a translocation involving the colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) gene, leading to overexpression of CSF1; a small population of neoplastic cells recruits large numbers of non-neoplastic CSF1-receptor-bearing inflammatory cells that make up the bulk of the lesion (a 'landscape' effect). Recurrent microhaemorrhage within the hypervascular synovium deposits haemosiderin, giving the tissue its pigmented appearance and the characteristic MRI blooming. The proliferative synovium erodes cartilage and subchondral bone, causing progressive joint destruction, particularly in the diffuse form.
additionalDifferentials: Rheumatoid or other chronic inflammatory synovitis
Synovial sarcoma or other malignant soft-tissue tumour
additionalInvestigations: MRI showing haemosiderin-laden synovium with low signal and blooming on gradient-echo sequences
Plain radiographs to assess soft-tissue swelling and juxta-articular bony erosions
Joint aspiration revealing serosanguineous or brown haemosiderin-stained fluid
Histological confirmation from synovial biopsy or resected tissue
Assessment of CSF1 overexpression where targeted therapy is being considered
redFlags: Rapid growth or atypical features raising concern for malignant transformation or sarcoma
Aggressive bony erosion and joint destruction in diffuse disease
Repeated recurrence after synovectomy indicating incomplete disease control
Neurovascular compromise from an expanding mass
reference.prognosis: The localised form has a good outcome after complete excision, whereas the diffuse form recurs frequently and can cause progressive joint destruction; malignant transformation is rare, and CSF1R-directed therapy has improved options for advanced disease.
pitfalls: Mistaking recurrent haemarthrosis for injury or a bleeding disorder and delaying diagnosis
Incomplete synovectomy in diffuse disease leading to recurrence
Overlooking the diagnosis when gradient-echo MRI sequences are not obtained
Confusing it with synovial chondromatosis or a malignant soft-tissue tumour
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
management: Undertake surgical synovectomy as the mainstay, with arthroscopic excision for localised nodular disease and open or combined complete synovectomy for the diffuse form
Consider CSF1R-directed systemic therapy such as pexidartinib for advanced, recurrent or unresectable diffuse disease, exploiting the underlying CSF1 overexpression
Use adjuvant radiosynovectomy or external-beam radiotherapy to reduce recurrence after incomplete resection of diffuse disease
Provide physiotherapy to restore range of motion and joint function postoperatively
Consider joint arthroplasty for end-stage cartilage and subchondral bone destruction
Monitor for local recurrence with serial MRI given the characteristic haemosiderin blooming, particularly in diffuse disease
Coordinate care across orthopaedic surgery, rheumatology and oncology for aggressive or recurrent tumours
